title: Lists and arrays
examples: What is the difference between a list and an array in programming?
How do I know which index to use when I want the last item?
Can I use a list to store different types of data?

explain.say: Today we are learning about lists and arrays in coding.
In programming, we store ordered collections of items in lists.
A very important rule to remember is that indexes start at zero.
To add a new item to an existing list, you use an add method.
We can use a loop to process every single item inside the list.
In real life, think about the days of the week in order.

faq.q: If I have five items, what is the index of the very first item?
faq.a: The first item will always have an index of zero. You can also ask what the starting index is.
asks: What is the index of the first element?
Does counting start at zero in programming?

faq.q: How do I add an item to the end of my list?
faq.a: Most languages have a specific method, like 'append', to add items to the end of the list. You might also ask how to extend the list.
asks: What command adds to the end?
How do I grow the list by one?

faq.q: What is the best way to look at every item in a list?
faq.a: Using a loop structure is the standard way to process every single item one by one. You could also ask how to iterate over the list.
asks: How do I check each item?
Can I use a loop for this?

faq.q: Does the index change if I add or remove items?
faq.a: Yes, if you remove an item, the indexes of all items after it will shift down by one. You might also ask about index shifting.
asks: If I delete something, what happens to the numbers?

faq.q: Can a list hold different types of data, like text and numbers?
faq.a: Yes, most programming lists can hold mixed data types, such as strings and integers together. You could also ask about heterogeneous lists.
asks: Can I mix text and numbers?
Is it okay to put different things in one list?

facts: Indexes in programming lists begin counting at zero.
You use an append or add method to increase the size of a list.
A loop structure allows you to perform an action for every item.
The index tells you the position, not the value, of an item.

quiz.say: If a list has three colors: red, blue, green. What is the index of the color blue?
quiz.why: Because indexing starts at zero, red is index zero, and blue is index one.

wrong.0: This is the index of the last item, green, not blue.
wrong.1: This number is too high for a list with only three items.
wrong.3: This is the index of the first item, red, not blue.

quiz.say: You have a list of scores: 85, 92, 78. If you add 99 to the end, what is the index of the new score?
quiz.why: The original items were at indices 0, 1, and 2. Adding one more item makes the last index three.

wrong.0: This index belongs to the second item, which did not change.
wrong.1: This is always the index of the very first item.
wrong.3: This was the index of the last item before you added the new score.

quiz.say: Which structure is best for processing every single element in a collection?
quiz.why: A loop is specifically designed to repeat an action for every item in a sequence.

wrong.0: Assigning only puts one value into one specific spot.
wrong.1: Comparing only checks if two things are the same or different.
wrong.2: Appending only adds a new item to the end of the list.
